n: This topic is devoted to examination of the corpse of a fetus and a newborn. Such an examination is carried out when there are signs of violent death or suspicion of it. The examination ends with taking material for laboratory examinations: mainly histological and forensic biological examinations are carried out. For histological examination, besides the internal organs, pieces of the placenta and umbilical cord are taken. Under the microscope, in a lung that has not breathed the alveoli are not expanded, whereas in one that has breathed they are expanded. This is used in determining live birth.

t: Cases in which examination is carried out
n: Now we look at the cases in which examination is carried out. An examination is ordered when the corpse of an infant of unknown mother is found. It is also carried out in stillbirth in a delivery outside a medical institution. Examination is also carried out when there is a complaint about the medical care given to a pregnant woman. The common condition of these cases is that there must be signs of violent death or suspicion of it.

The questions put to the examination are of a special nature and differ from the questions in other examinations of corpses. They fall into four directions. The first is the state of birth: whether the infant is newborn and whether it was born alive. The second is age and viability: what the gestational age is and whether it is viable. The third is duration of life: if born alive, how long it lived. The fourth is care: whether the infant received proper care. The usual questions are also put. Attention: newborn and live-born are not the same concept; in forensic medicine the newborn period is the first 24 hours.

t: Additional questions: cause of death and injuries
n: Besides the special questions peculiar to an infant, the general questions of other corpse examinations are also put. The expert is asked to determine the cause and time of death. The presence or absence of bodily injuries and the mechanism of their infliction are also determined. Remember: for law enforcement agencies the exact cause of death is more important than distinguishing active from passive killing.

t: Case analysis: discovery of a corpse
n: Now let us consider a case analysis. Situation: the corpse of an infant of unknown mother is found. In such a case, examination is ordered on suspicion of violent death. The first questions are as follows: whether the infant is newborn, whether it was born alive, and what the gestational age, that is the age of the fetus, is. The following questions: whether it is viable, how long it lived and whether it was cared for. Question for the student: which of the list must be resolved first and why? Think about your answer.

The concept of the newborn differs in different sciences. In forensic medicine this period is 24 hours, in paediatrics, that is the neonatal period, 4 weeks, and in obstetrics and gynaecology 7 days. The meaning in forensic medicine differs from that in paediatrics and obstetrics-gynaecology. This is tied to the law: Article 99 of the Criminal Code, that is the CC, singles out intentional killing by the mother during childbirth. If another person kills, this is classified as intentional homicide under Article 97 of the CC.

t: Legal significance of the newborn period
n: We dwell on the legal significance of the newborn period. In forensic medicine the newborn period is the first 24 hours, and this feature is tied to the requirements of legislation. Article 99 of the CC separately singles out intentional killing by the mother of her child during childbirth or immediately after birth, and the punishment is much milder than for intentional homicide. Childbirth lasts approximately about a day. Because of pain and her psycho-emotional state, the mother may harm the child without fully realising it. If another person performs the same act, it is classified under Article 97 of the CC as intentional homicide.

t: Quick question: duration of the newborn period
n: Quick question: how long does the newborn period last in paediatrics, obstetrics-gynaecology and forensic medicine? In paediatrics it is four weeks after birth, that is the neonatal period. In obstetrics-gynaecology it is seven days. In forensic medicine this period is the first 24 hours. Attention, there is a risk of error: 4 weeks, 7 days and 24 hours are not equal to each other. Do not confuse the forensic medical period with the paediatric period.

Looking at the signs of the newborn as a whole, they are as follows: traces of blood on the body, vernix caseosa, caput succedaneum, meconium, umbilical cord and atelectasis of the lungs. But only atelectasis and the signs on the umbilical cord are regarded as absolute, that is fully reliable: primary atelectasis of the lungs, absence or initial signs of the demarcation ring, and an umbilical cord not yet detached. The remaining signs are relative; they may be found on the 2nd day of life and later.

t: Traces of blood and vernix caseosa
n: If there are no external injuries, traces of blood on the body are regarded as a sign of the newborn: they arise from rupture of the soft tissues of the birth canal. Attention: when the infant's body is washed, the traces of blood disappear. Vernix caseosa is a whitish-grey semi-liquid mass consisting of a mixture of sebaceous gland secretion, desquamated epidermis, lanugo hair and amniotic fluid. The vernix protects the fetal skin from maceration in amniotic fluid; there is more in the folds, and if not washed off it persists for up to a week.

Caput succedaneum, in a narrow pelvis and weak labour, most often appears on the head, sometimes in the buttock area. It is soft, and on section reddish-yellow. Attention: caput succedaneum is not a cephalohaematoma; the difference lies in location and time of resorption. Caput succedaneum arises from disturbance of local circulation, is also found in the projection of the sutures, its content is serous fluid with blood, and it is resorbed in 2–3 days. A cephalohaematoma, by contrast, arises from haemorrhage under the periosteum, lies on the bone, is limited by the sutures, and is resorbed in 2 weeks or more.

t: Meconium and signs of the umbilical cord
n: Meconium, that is the first stool, is a dark-green semi-liquid mass, found in the large intestine, around the anus, buttocks and thighs; it contains mucus and bile pigment. Meconium is usually completely passed from the intestine within 1–2 days after birth, and in premature infants this period extends to 3–4 days. In a newborn the umbilical cord is moist, glistening, whitish-pinkish; then it dries and shrivels, becomes brownish-yellow, then brownish-black. In live birth, at the base of the cord a reddish demarcation ring appears after a few hours, sometimes at the end of day 1; on days 5–7 the cord separates.

A lung that has not breathed is in a state of primary atelectasis. Such an infant can live only a few seconds. Absolute signs: primary atelectasis of the lungs, absence or initial signs of the demarcation ring, and an undetached umbilical cord. The remaining signs are relative in nature and may be found on the second and following days of the infant's life. Attention: an absolute and a relative sign are not the same. In an unwashed infant vernix caseosa persists for up to a week, so it is not the sole evidence.

t: Case analysis: signs of the newborn
n: Case analysis. Situation: the umbilical cord is moist, glistening, whitish-pinkish, and not separated from the body and placenta; around the anus there is a dark-green mass, that is meconium. An umbilical cord not separated from the body and placenta is an absolute sign, so the infant is regarded as newborn. Meconium is usually completely passed from the intestine within 1–2 days after birth, and in premature infants this period extends to 3–4 days; meconium is a relative sign. Question: what can be said if there is a demarcation ring on the cord? The ring appears after a few hours, sometimes at the end of day 1, and the cord separates on days 5–7.

The criteria of live birth have been set by the World Health Organization, that is the WHO: breathing outside the mother's body, heartbeat, pulsation of the umbilical cord or voluntary movements. However, in forensic medicine, methods of determining heartbeat, cord pulsation and voluntary movement after death have not yet been developed. Therefore the question of live birth is resolved mainly by determining whether the infant breathed. Under the microscope, in a lung that has breathed the alveoli are expanded and the epithelium is flat. If it has not breathed, the alveoli are not expanded and the epithelium is cuboidal.

The lung test is named after Galen–Raugier–Schreyer. The test was first used in forensic medical practice in 1681 by I. Schreyer. A lung that has not breathed is heavier than water, its specific gravity 1.05–1.06; in a lung that has breathed this figure is below 1.0. Stages: first ligatures are applied, then the complex is placed in a vessel of water. If it sinks, the lung is placed separately, then the lobes and pieces. If negative, the lung, lobes and pieces are placed separately; with a positive result the test is stopped.

t: False results of the lung test
n: The lung test may give a false result. False positive cases: a putrefied corpse, a lung that has been artificially ventilated, and a frozen lung that has not thawed well. A piece floated by putrefactive gas, if squeezed by hand under water, does not float up again; a fully thawed frozen lung sinks. A false negative result occurs in secondary atelectasis: a lung that has previously breathed collapses because of inflammation or closure of the airways. Then the method of Taranukhin (1907) or Trakhtenberg (1958) is used: a piece is placed in a flask under reduced pressure, and the piece with atelectasis floats up.

The gastrointestinal test is associated with the name of Breslau. In breathing, part of the air passes through the oesophagus into the stomach and intestines; the test is based on this (W. Breslau, 1865). Ligatures are applied to the entrance and exit of the stomach, to the air-containing parts of the intestine and to the rectum, and the organs are placed in water. The air-containing area floats, and when pricked bubbles emerge. Air passes gradually: if only in the stomach, the infant lived less than 3 hours; after 6 hours air passes into the large intestine. Putrefactive gases and artificial respiration give a false positive result, so in such cases the test is not recommended.

t: The radiological test and its limitation
n: The radiological test is based on determining the presence of air in the lungs, stomach and intestines before the corpse is opened. It was proposed in 1939 by Ya. G. Dillon. However, X-ray cannot distinguish a lung that has breathed from an artificially ventilated lung and from a state with putrefactive gases. It requires special equipment, and its possibilities are limited. Therefore it is not used in the practice of forensic medical examination now.

We review the tests with quick questions. What result does the lung test give in a putrefied corpse? A false positive, since putrefactive gases make the lung float. What is the result in secondary atelectasis? A false negative; the method of Taranukhin (1907) or its modification by Trakhtenberg (1958) is recommended. Is the gastrointestinal test reliable in artificial respiration? No, air also enters the stomach, and the test is not recommended. Attention: false positive and false negative are not the same; in the first a dead lung floats, in the second a lung that has breathed sinks.

Macroscopic signs help to distinguish the live-born from the stillborn. A lung that has breathed almost fills the chest, is elastic, and on squeezing frothy blood is released. A lung that has not breathed is small, dense and close to the spine; on squeezing a little blood is released. In the live-born the chest is barrel-shaped, the dome of the diaphragm at the level of ribs VI–VII, the lung marbled, weight 85–90 g. In the stillborn, however, the chest is flat, the dome at the level of ribs IV–V, the lung uniformly bluish dark red, weight 55–60 g. In live birth putrefaction begins in the respiratory organs, in stillbirth usually at the natural orifices.

t: Histology: the lung that has not breathed
n: The histology of a lung that has not breathed is distinctive. In the lung of a stillborn infant the alveoli are not expanded, that is air has not entered and the lumen has not opened. The alveolar epithelium is cuboidal, and the interalveolar septa are thick. The elastic fibres lie in bundles, and there is no blood in the capillaries. Attention: there are no hyaline membranes in a lung that has not breathed. In small and medium arteries "bud-like" and "cushion-like" protrusions are seen.

t: Histology: the lung that has breathed
n: In a lung that has breathed the alveoli are expanded, the septa are thinned, and the alveolar epithelium is flat. The capillaries are congested. Compare this with the lung that has not breathed: there the alveoli are not expanded, the epithelium is cuboidal, the septa are thick, and there is no blood in the capillaries. Attention: cuboidal epithelium and flat epithelium are not the same. The first is characteristic of a lung that has not breathed, the second of one that has.

Composition of hyaline membranes: blood proteins that have seeped out of the pulmonary capillaries, that is albumin, globulin and fibrin. They lie on the inner surface of the alveoli. They are so named because they stain like hyaline cartilage. For their formation the infant must live at least 1–2 hours; they are usually found in those who lived a few hours. They occur mainly in live-born premature infants, and are absent in a lung that has not breathed. For this reason they are useful in assessing the duration of life.

In stillborn infants, "bud-like" and "cushion-like" protrusions are found inside the small and medium-calibre pulmonary arteries; this is Mityaeva's sign, 1970. In a lung that has breathed such protrusions are not seen. Therefore this sign helps to confirm under the microscope that the infant did not breathe. For histological examination, pieces are taken from the internal organs of the corpse, and also from the placenta and umbilical cord. Attention: Mityaeva's sign is characteristic of a lung that has not breathed, whereas hyaline membranes are found in an infant that has breathed, that is was born alive.

Case analysis on histological examination. Case 1: on the lung section the alveoli are not expanded, the epithelium is cuboidal, the septa are thick, there is no blood in the capillaries, and there are bud-like protrusions in the arteries. Case 2: the alveoli are expanded, the epithelium is flat, the septa are thin, the capillaries are congested, and the elastic fibres are arranged regularly. In addition: if hyaline membranes are found on the inner surface of the alveoli, the infant has usually lived a few hours. Question: in which case was the infant live-born, in which stillborn? Justify the answer with microscopic signs.

In terms of gestational age, term and maturity must be distinguished. Term is the sum of features showing that the pregnancy lasted on average 10 lunar months, that is 280 days. According to WHO recommendation, birth at 37–42 weeks is regarded as timely; those born then are called full-term. The body length of a full-term infant is on average 50–54 cm and weight 3000–3500 g. The body length of a mature infant is 45 cm or more, and weight not less than 2500 g. Attention: term and maturity are not the same.

Gestational age is determined mainly by anthropometry and certain signs. Haase's formula gives the result in months of pregnancy: in the first half the square root of the length is taken, in the second half the length is divided by 5. For example, 16 cm corresponds to 4 months, 40 cm to 8 months. The Baltazard–Dervieux method gives age in days: body length must be multiplied by 5.6, for example 40 cm × 5.6 = 224 days, that is 8 months. Yakupov's method gives it in months of pregnancy: the head circumference is divided by 3.4, for example 34 cm ÷ 3.4 = 10 months.

t: Placenta, umbilical cord and ossification centres
n: The placenta, umbilical cord and ossification centres also help assess age. Cord length and placental weight in month VI are 38 cm and 250 g, in month X 50 cm and 500 g. In the intermediate months: in month VII 42 cm and 340 g; in month VIII 46 cm and 410 g; in month IX 47 cm and 470 g. Ossification centres: the lower epiphysis of the femur, that is Béclard's nucleus, appears in month IX of pregnancy, diameter 0.5–0.7 cm; the calcaneus in month V, 0.8–1.1 cm; the talus in month VII, 0.7–1.0 cm. Pathology, smoking, alcohol and narcotics may delay the appearance of the centres or stop it altogether.

Viability is the infant's ability to live outside the mother's body. A live-born infant may also be non-viable. WHO criterion: an infant of length less than 25 cm and weight less than 500 g is non-viable because of extreme prematurity. In this case the corpse is not opened: external examination is made and weight and length are measured. Defects such as anencephaly and a two-chambered heart are incompatible with life. If an external defect is found, for example a sixth finger or cleft lip, the brain and internal organs are examined. In birth trauma, injuries incompatible with life are possible: crushing of the brain, fracture of the cervical vertebrae with damage to the spinal cord.

t: Duration of life outside the mother's body
n: We assess the duration of life outside the mother's body by the time of appearance of the signs. The demarcation ring forms by the end of the first day. Hyaline membranes form when the infant has lived at least 1–2 hours. Secondary atelectasis of the lungs develops no earlier than after 5–6 hours. Caput succedaneum is resorbed on days 2–3. Meconium is also passed by the end of the first day; jaundice begins on days 2–3 and passes on days 1–10. If air is only in the stomach, the infant lived less than 3 hours; after 5–6 hours it passes into the small intestine, after 6 hours into the large. Attention: the times are approximate, and the conclusion relies not on one sign but on many.

t: Care of the infant and causes of death
n: Care of the infant and causes of death. Signs of care: the infant is swaddled, has clothing, the cord has been cut and tied, the body has been cleaned of blood and vernix caseosa, and there is milk in the stomach. Antenatal non-violent death often results from asphyxia related to the placenta or umbilical cord. The main cause of intranatal death is birth trauma, in which there is no external injury. Postnatal violent death is of two kinds: in the active kind, strangulation, closing of the airways, drowning; in the passive kind the infant is left without care, that is bleeding, cold, hunger. Attention: for law enforcement agencies it is important to state the exact cause of death, not the active or passive type.

Antenatal non-violent death is mainly from intrauterine asphyxia. Causes on the part of the placenta: its praevia, infarction or premature separation. Compression of the umbilical cord, wrapping around the neck or a true knot also lead to asphyxia. For this reason the placenta and umbilical cord are examined. On the fetal corpse, signs of rapidly occurring death, aspiration of amniotic fluid and much meconium in the fluid are found. Maternal diseases are also causes: acute infections, syphilis, decompensated heart disease, toxaemia and malformations.

The main cause of non-violent death in the intranatal period is birth trauma. In a narrow pelvis, a large fetus or weak labour, the head is compressed for a long time, the bones of the vault of the skull fracture and haemorrhage occurs into the cranial cavity. The parietal and frontal bones are most often injured; the haemorrhage is severe in rupture of the tentorium cerebelli and falx. In birth trauma no external injury or wound is formed. If a woman helps with her hands, abrasions, bruises and a tear at the corner of the mouth occur on the face and neck. This is how the two types of injury are distinguished.

t: Features of the examination and collecting material
n: We consider the features of the examination and the procedure for collecting material. In external examination, clothing, anthropometry, traces of blood, vernix caseosa, meconium and ossification centres are studied; the placenta and umbilical cord are also examined. Internal examination begins with the chest and abdominal cavities. The bones of the skull are cut with scissors to form windows, and the falx and tentorium are left whole. To determine live birth, flotation tests of the lungs and gastrointestinal tract are carried out; attention is paid to milk in the stomach and meconium in the large intestine. At the end, material is taken for histological and forensic biological examination, that is blood group testing; for histology, pieces are taken from organs, placenta and umbilical cord.

Internal examination and incision technique. It is recommended to begin the internal examination with the chest and abdominal cavities. To study the oral cavity and palate, the main midline incision starts not from the chin but from the lower lip. So as not to damage the integrity of the umbilical vessels, the incision is not carried to the navel but continued to both sides toward the pubic ligaments. In the cranial cavity, the frontal, parietal and temporal bones are cut with scissors to form windows; the falx, sinuses and tentorium cerebelli are left whole.

Case analysis on collecting material. Situation: the corpse of an infant of unknown mother is found. External and internal examination is finished, and what remains is to take material for the laboratory. For histological examination, besides the internal organs, pieces of the placenta and umbilical cord are taken. Attention: the group identity of blood is determined by forensic biological examination, and it is carried out separately from the histological one. Question: why are the placenta and umbilical cord examined in addition to the corpse? The causes of antenatal death may be visible in them.

We summarise. In forensic medicine the newborn period is the first 24 hours; this differs from the period in paediatrics and obstetrics. Live birth is resolved mainly by whether the infant breathed, and under the microscope in a lung that has breathed the alveoli are expanded. For hyaline membranes the infant must live at least 1–2 hours, and secondary atelectasis develops no earlier than after 5–6 hours. Review questions: list the signs of the newborn; which signs are absolute; how is the lung test performed in secondary atelectasis?
